claims.statement: At the target job shape the ledger write rate stays below 10% of the measured GCS durable-write ceiling (~260/s same-key, ~593/s aggregate) with no measurable regression in GCS p99 for other components

notes.note: Testable half PROVEN: a usable band exists and is now mapped. At 10% of the 262 writes/s same-key ceiling with redo capped at 1% of N, 18 of 24 (rate, N) points admit a usable W. Breaking points: N=1000 loses all feasible W above ~100 units/s, N=50000 above ~1000/s, N=10^6 above ~10^4/s. That is the band the design doc predicted, now with numbers. Untestable half - no measurable regression in GCS p99 for other components - needs a real cluster and stays open.
Second half still open; the stage-C rig is single-node and in-process, so GCS p99 under load for other components was not measured. Would need a loaded multi-component cluster.

SECOND HALF NOW PROVEN, closing the claim. The first half (a usable band exists) was proven in stage B; the p99-regression half had been open since iteration 7 because it needed a real cluster. Result: at the design rate of 26 writes/s the victim's internal_kv p99 moved +3.0 percent and p95 +1.7 percent, against a measured noise floor of 9.8 percent (2 sigma over six interleaved baselines, mean 3.288 ms). Nothing regressed anywhere up to 200 writes/s: deltas were +3.0, +2.0, +3.2 and +20.2 percent at 26, 50, 100 and 200/s, all below the 25 percent threshold. THE RESULT IS ONLY MEANINGFUL BECAUSE THE RIG PROVED IT CAN SEE A REGRESSION: an INDEPENDENT positive control that does not involve the ledger at all - four loaders writing 4 MB values - moved p99 from 3.11 ms to 132.1 ms, a factor of 42. Two earlier attempts were void or uncertain and the progression matters. Attempt 1 was blind: the victim slept 10ms between ops so it measured wake-up jitter, arms ran sequentially so warm-up dominated, and the noise floor (43 percent) exceeded the effect size; its overload arm even produced LOWER p95 and actor latency than idle, which is not a physical result. Attempt 2 fixed the victim and interleaved the baselines, and its positive control fired, but the floor was 26.2 percent - marginally above the pre-registered 25 percent - so it was recorded as uncertain rather than rounded up to a pass. Attempt 3 lengthened the arms to 60s (about 53,000 samples each) which cut the floor to 9.8 percent. NOTE that attempt 2's apparent finding that regression begins between 26/s and 200/s was itself baseline noise: at proper resolution 200/s does not regress.

claims.statement: A detached, named, non-head-pinned coordinator survives driver death and head pod replacement under gcs_storage=rocksdb, and is reattachable by name from a new driver
claims.refutes_if: after head restart the actor is dead, duplicated, or the name lookup fails

notes.note: The driver-death half is PROVEN on real Ray: a detached named coordinator created by a subprocess driver executed all 40 units AFTER that driver called os._exit(0), and a fresh driver reattached by name and observed the progress. Resume also proven end-to-end: ray.kill the coordinator, and the restarted incarnation claimed epoch 2, resumed_from=40 and executed ZERO further units - the ledger did exactly its job. The HEAD POD REPLACEMENT half is untested and untestable here; it needs KubeRay. Recorded as uncertain rather than proven because that half is the harder one.

Split result, and the split is the useful part. SURVIVED: the ledger (60 committed units recovered intact), the actor NAME (coord-H still registered after the head restart, so GCS reloaded it from tables), and progress off-head before the kill. FAILED: reattach, with ActorUnschedulableError - 'The node specified via NodeAffinitySchedulingStrategy does not exist any more, and soft=False was specified'. So the coordinator was not lost; it became UNSCHEDULABLE because it was HARD-pinned to a node id that no longer exists. Fixable (soft=True or no affinity) and tracked as C25. Stays uncertain because the harness restarted the whole cluster rather than only the head.

C25's run removes the schedulability blocker: with soft or no affinity the coordinator IS restarted after its node is destroyed and DOES recover its ledger state (epoch 1->2, resumed_from=60, zero redo). But C4 stays uncertain, and now for a precise reason rather than a vague one. C4's refutation condition has three clauses - dead, DUPLICATED, or name lookup fails - and this harness can only test two. Because it does 'ray stop --force', the old coordinator process is guaranteed dead before the head returns, which is exactly the condition under which duplication is impossible. A real KubeRay head-pod replacement leaves the worker raylet and the old coordinator ALIVE while GCS reloads the actor table, and that is the only situation in which two live incarnations could coexist. The harsh test therefore does NOT subsume the gentle one: it destroys the hazard it is meant to detect. Closing C4 needs the same harness change as C7 - restart gcs_server in place.

PROVEN across the two decomposed failure modes, with the scope stated explicitly rather than glossed. C4's three clauses are dead / duplicated / name lookup fails, and no single harness reaches all three, because the hazards are mutually exclusive: duplication requires the old coordinator to be ALIVE, and unschedulability requires its node to be GONE. Two runs together cover them. (1) runs/20260910-061819-C25pin - node destroyed: the coordinator is rescheduled onto a surviving node, re-runs __init__, claims epoch 2 and recovers all 60 committed units with zero redo, provided it is not hard-pinned. Covers 'dead' and 'name lookup'. (2) this run - node survives, gcs_server killed and restarted in place: exactly ONE live actor row, NumRestarts=0, epoch unchanged at 1, the same instance id before and after, ledger contiguous with no duplicates. Covers 'duplicated', which was previously unreachable because ray stop --force guaranteed the old coordinator was dead. From the coordinator's point of view a KubeRay head-pod replacement IS one of these two cases depending on whether its own node is replaced with the head. Residual, and deliberately not claimed: a real head pod comes back on a NEW IP, whereas the re-exec'd gcs_server reused its address. That dimension is raylet-to-GCS reconnection, which KubeRay's own GCS-FT machinery owns (stable head Service DNS plus gcs_rpc_server_reconnect_timeout_s); it is not a property of R4's design and R4 makes no claim about it.

claims.statement: Coordinator state is fully reconstructible from ledger + live-cluster introspection, with no external storage
claims.refutes_if: some necessary state is neither in the ledger nor re-derivable from the cluster

notes.note: The ledger half is demonstrated end to end: a restarted coordinator reconstructed its full progress from internal_kv alone, resumed_from=40, and executed zero redundant units with no external storage. The other half is NOT demonstrated - the reference implementation does not do Serve-style two-source reconciliation against live cluster state, because its work units are stateless tasks with nothing to reconcile. A coordinator owning long-lived child actors would need it, and that is where C5 could still fail.

PROVEN, conditionally, and the condition is a concrete design requirement rather than a caveat: child actors must be named DETERMINISTICALLY from job scope plus index. Rig: a phase-1 driver creates K=6 detached named children and records only R=2 into the ledger before os._exit(1), so four crashes land in the dangerous create->crash->record window. NEGATIVE CONTROL (opaque uuid4 names, ledger the only link) fired exactly as required: 4 genuine orphans still alive plus 4 genuine duplicates with distinct new pids. With scope-prefixed names, both recovery paths were clean - explicit listing adopted all 6 with unchanged pids and created nothing, and get_if_exists=True re-acquired the 4 unrecorded children with unchanged pids and no listing pass at all. So reality is self-describing when names carry attribution, and the ledger is only needed for intent. IMPORTANT SCOPE NOTE discovered while fixing a void run: Ray REQUIRES detached actors to be named, so the fully unattributable case cannot even be constructed - every leaked child is at least discoverable, and what opaque naming loses is only the ability to tell WHOSE it is. Caveat for the design: get_if_exists=True returns the actor but does not report whether it adopted or created, so a coordinator that needs to distinguish 'resume this child's state' from 'initialize a fresh one' still needs the explicit path.

claims.statement: GCS unavailability during head failover degrades to 'work continues, durability pauses' without deadlocking the coordinator or tripping the GCS health check
claims.refutes_if: a failover window causes coordinator deadlock, unbounded queue growth, or GCS NOT_SERVING

notes.note: raised: ray#55996 (OPEN P1) shows DEADLINE_EXCEEDED is not retried by the GCS client and wedges the caller; grpc_util.h:127-133

Blocked on infrastructure, not on ideas. Needs GCS to be restarted IN PLACE while the coordinator keeps running, which a single-node in-process ray.init cannot do - shutting it down takes the coordinator with it. Fidelity gap F3 already records that the stage-A rig models GCS restart as ops failing and then succeeding rather than as a process restart. Requires KubeRay or a multi-process cluster where the head can be killed independently.

REFUTED as stated, in the benign direction. The design assumed a GCS outage degrades to 'work continues, durability pauses'. It does not: work pauses too. With gcs_server SIGKILLed in place (raylets and coordinator untouched), executed_this_incarnation froze at 48 and ledger writes at 49 for the whole 35s outage, then rose to 327/328 after gcs_server was re-exec'd with its captured argv. The cause is structural, not incidental: commit() is a synchronous internal_kv put on the unit loop's critical path, so the loop can advance at most W-1 units past a blocked commit and then stops. The measurement is trustworthy because the two signals were separated - progress() touches no KV and kept answering (1 sampler error in the whole run), while info() went red with GetTimeoutError exactly during the outage. So the flat line is a measurement of 'not working', not of a blind sampler. Both controls fired: the nokill arm rose monotonically throughout (exec 5->400, writes 49->401) and NC-sampler saw KV go red. GOOD NEWS on the dangerous half: ray#55996 did NOT reproduce. The blocked put recovered on its own once GCS returned; no wedge, no restart (NumRestarts=0, epoch stayed 1), 336 units committed contiguous with no duplicates.

claims.statement: Resume boundary is intra-cluster: the design survives driver and head loss but not RayCluster replacement, and KubeRay's RayJob retry path cannot be configured to preserve the cluster
claims.refutes_if: KubeRay can be configured to retry the driver without recreating the cluster (refutation is the good outcome here)

notes.note: REFUTED, and this claim was written so refutation is the GOOD outcome. KubeRay's SubmitterConfig.BackoffLimit in SidecarMode with SidecarSubmitterRestart is 'the maximum container restart count' - the submitter runs as a container in the head pod and is restarted in place, so the DRIVER dies and the RayCluster does not. Separately, spec.clusterSelector targets a pre-existing long-lived RayCluster. R4's resume boundary is therefore wider than the parent doc assumed, and the KubeRay-side lifecycle R4 needs already exists. RayJob.spec.backoffLimit does still recreate the cluster ('Each retry creates a new RayCluster'), so that clause of C9 stands.

claims.statement: Scoping ledger keys by session_name prevents a new cluster that reuses an existing gcs_storage_path from adopting a stale ledger, given the KV DB's cluster-id guard is disabled
claims.refutes_if: session_name is not stable across head restarts, or a stale ledger from a prior cluster can still be adopted despite the scoping

notes.note: HALF the claim is settled, and it is recorded as uncertain rather than proven because of the other half. notes.note: REFUTED on clause 2, its own stated terms. Clauses 1 and 3 held: with Q=8 batches the coordinator completed 25 units during a 35s GCS outage against the sync baseline's ZERO, the queue saturated exactly at Q as required by NC-queue-bound, and every arm's ledger stayed contiguous and duplicate-free with no writer errors. But the redo window came out at 30 units against the stated bound of Q*W + W = 27. The excess is fully explained and that is what makes it a refutation rather than noise: at the moment of death the queue held 8 batches (24 units), the writer had ALREADY DEQUEUED one batch and was blocked committing it (+3), and the producer had filled its next batch and was blocked in q.put (+3). 24+3+3 = 30, exactly what was measured. So the real bound is Q*W + 2W, not Q*W + W: I counted the buffer but not the two batches in flight on either side of it. Per the rule adopted after C1->C16 and C2->C22 the condition is NOT widened after the fact - the corrected bound is split out as C27 and must be proven on its own terms, by a sweep over Q rather than by a single point. Sync baseline behaved exactly as predicted (redo 3 = W, backlog 3), which confirms the metric is measuring the queue and not something else. Reaching this at all required the coordinator to die MID-OUTAGE with the queue full: ray.kill goes through the GCS actor manager, which is precisely what is unavailable then, so the coordinator kills itself via a cached actor handle from the pre-existing sampler.

claims.statement: A coordinator that crashes while GCS is unavailable does not thrash: with max_restarts=-1 the restart storm is bounded, and the compaction sweep keeps the ledger key count bounded even though the epoch counter climbs

notes.note: PROVEN on all three clauses, within an envelope that this run also measured. There is NO restart storm: across a sweep of outage durations 0/10/30s the coordinator restarted exactly ONCE in every arm, max_epoch=2, NumRestarts=1, ledger_key_count=3, redo <= 3 units = W, contiguous and duplicate-free. The negative control (die with GCS healthy) was green as required at exactly one restart. THE CLAIM WAS RAISED ON A MISREADING OF MY OWN RIG, and the first attempt at this experiment proved it: runs/20260910-...-C28storm is VOID because the control churned HARDER than the treatment arms (epoch 14 vs 11-12), which is anti-correlated with outage duration and therefore cannot be caused by the outage. Cause: JobCoordinator is declared max_task_retries=-1, and die() called os._exit inline so the task was in flight when the actor died; Ray replayed it on every restart, giving an infinite suicide loop for as long as the calling sampler stayed alive. Iteration 16's epochs=[18] has the identical cause. So R4 does not thrash; my rig did. ENVELOPE: the 60s arm could not be measured because the CLUSTER ITSELF DIED - a GCS outage at or beyond gcs_rpc_server_reconnect_timeout_s (default 60s) makes the raylet give up and the node exit, so there is no coordinator left to restart. Split out as C29. GENERAL DESIGN CONSTRAINT discovered here and not currently in the doc: max_task_retries=-1 REPLAYS in-flight tasks on a restarted actor, so every coordinator method must be idempotent under replay, not just run().

claims.statement: A GCS outage at or beyond gcs_rpc_server_reconnect_timeout_s (60s default) terminates the cluster rather than the coordinator, and R4 degrades to a cold restart on the same rocksdb path with zero data loss and zero redo
claims.refutes_if: the ledger is lost or corrupted after the cluster dies, or a cold restart on the same storage path redoes committed work, or the epoch counter fails to advance for the new incarnation

notes.note: Proven on all three clauses by the outage_60 arm plus probe_outage_ceiling.py, whose output is saved in the run directory. The cluster died (raylet gave up on GCS past the 60s reconnect timeout; the follow-up driver could not even ray.init). The ledger did not: a cold restart on the same gcs_storage_path recovered 45 committed units, contiguous and duplicate-free, 3 ledger keys, the actor name still registered from tables/, and a fresh incarnation reporting resumed_from=45 with executed_this_incarnation=0. Zero redo, reproduced twice. The epoch advanced correctly to 3 on the second cold restart; the first reported epoch 2 because GCS had RESTORED the detached actor from tables/ and get_if_exists returned that same incarnation - which is the correct fencing behaviour, since a restored actor must not claim a second epoch for itself. So R4's worst case is DOWNTIME bounded by cold-restart time, not data loss and not redo. That is a better degradation than the design assumed and it is the direct payoff of putting the ledger in rocksdb.

claims.statement: The async redo window is Q*W + W + p, where p in [1,W] is the partial batch held by the producer at the instant of death; so Q*W + 2W is a tight upper bound and measured redo VARIES across repeats at fixed Q
claims.refutes_if: repeated runs at fixed Q all yield an identical redo, or any measured redo falls outside the interval Q*W + W + 1 to Q*W + 2W

notes.note: REFUTED on its deciding clause. Six repeats at Q=8, identical except for the moment of death swept across the batch phase (25.0 to 31.5s into the outage), returned redo=30 EVERY TIME, p=3 every time, all six saturated, all contiguous. There is no variation, so the interval story is wrong and Q*W + 2W is not a bound with slack - it is the value. The pre-registration named this outcome in advance and stated the consequence: if the repeats are constant then Q=16's 53 needs a different explanation entirely, and the redo bound cannot be trusted until that explanation is found. It is now found, and it is a control defect of mine. Reconstructing Q=16: durable 45 + queue 48 + writer 3 = 96, executed 98, so p=2 and the producer was NOT blocked in q.put - it was still executing units, with the third unit of its batch in flight. The queue takes 51 units to reach the blocked state at Q=16 versus 27 at Q=8, and at the measured throughput that lands almost exactly at the +30s death mark. So the Q=16 arm died BEFORE the producer had blocked. My saturation control checked queued == Q, which is necessary but NOT SUFFICIENT: a full queue does not imply a blocked producer. Split out as C31, whose control must observe the producer actually blocked.

claims.statement: Once the producer is actually blocked on a full queue, the async redo window is exactly Q*W + 2W, deterministically and independent of when the crash lands; a smaller redo means the producer had not yet blocked, not that the bound is loose
claims.refutes_if: a death taken well after the producer blocks yields redo other than Q*W + 2W at any Q, or the Q=16 arm still yields 53 when death is delayed past its blocking point

notes.note: PROVEN, and it resolves the three-claim arc C27 -> C30 -> C31 with one distinction: the formula was always right, the measurements were taken in the wrong STATE. Three arms, every prediction hit. q16_early (the negative control, death at +30s) reproduced the anomaly EXACTLY - redo 53, p=2, producer_blocked False - so C27 was not refuted by noise and the reasoning stands. q16_late (same Q, death at +45s) gave exactly 54 = Q*W + 2W with p=3 and producer_blocked True. q32_late was included as a deliberate second instance of the trap, predicted in advance to come out BELOW 102 because Q=32 needs 99 units to reach the blocked state and a 55s outage does not supply them; it gave 96 with queued=31, never even filling the queue. So: the redo window is deterministic at Q*W + 2W once the producer is actually blocked, and any smaller measurement means the pipeline had not yet stalled. THE CONTROL DEFECT that caused all of this is now explicit: queued == Q is necessary but NOT SUFFICIENT for a blocked producer, because the producer can have just completed the put that filled the queue and moved on. The rig now derives producer_blocked from the coordinator's own state at death (p == W) and only blocked arms count as evidence. DESIGN CONSEQUENCE: Q is not freely choosable. Q must be small enough that Q*W + W units are produced within the outage you intend to ride out, otherwise the buffer is never fully used and the redo bound is not the operative limit.

claims.statement: An adaptive coalescing policy that sizes W from the observed completion rate to hold a target ledger WRITE RATE bounds both the write rate and the redo TIME window across a varying workload, whereas any single fixed W can bound only one of them
claims.refutes_if: adaptive misses the target write rate by more than 20 percent at some completion rate, or its worst-case redo exceeds that of a fixed W achieving the same write rate, or a single fixed W matches adaptive on every profile (adaptivity buys nothing)

notes.note: REFUTED on clause 2, robustly, and the refutation carries a real design insight. The negative control tied EXACTLY on the constant profile (0.0 percent difference on both metrics), so the fixed baseline was not mistuned. At the pre-registered tau=5s adaptive also failed clause 1, missing the 20 percent write-rate target on the ramp profile at 25.1 percent - but I swept tau from 0.5 to 60s before concluding, precisely so the refutation would not be of a strawman, and tau=60s does hold the rate (worst deviation 16.4 percent). Clause 2 fails anyway and cannot be tuned away: on the ramp profile adaptive's worst-case redo is 13-18 UNITS against fixed_mean's 4, while fixed_mean achieves an equivalent write rate (18.0 vs 16.4 percent deviation). So adaptive does not dominate; it TRADES. What it buys is redo TIME - 0.026s on the ramp against fixed_mean's 0.80s and fixed_peak's 3.80s, a factor of 30 to 145. THE INSIGHT: the two policies optimise different denominators. Fixed W bounds the redo COUNT; adaptive bounds the redo WALL-CLOCK. They are the same quantity divided by the completion rate, so neither can bound both while the rate varies. R4's budgets (C2 on write count, C10 on at-least-once units) are denominated in UNITS, which is the denominator fixed W already bounds. RECOMMENDATION: keep fixed W. Adopt adaptive only if a deployment's redo budget is stated in seconds rather than units, and then with a long tau around 60s. Idea buried.
